text: A pipeline that works today and a pipeline someone can trust next month are different things. This lesson adds the two kinds of monitoring Driftwood's platform actually needs: knowing when the daily run breaks, and knowing before the warehouse bill becomes a surprise.

A resource monitor on DRIFTWOOD_ETL_WH sets a fifty-credit monthly quota -- deliberately generous for a once-daily batch job. It notifies at seventy-five percent and actually suspends the warehouse at one hundred, catching a runaway query or a forgotten debugging session before it becomes a cost surprise at month-end.
Creating that monitor is a real, ordinary Snowflake statement -- the same CREATE RESOURCE MONITOR mechanism shown here, applied to Driftwood's own ETL warehouse.

On the Airflow side, one retry with a ten-minute delay handles a transient connection hiccup quietly. on_failure_callback is what actually matters for trust: if the DAG fails after retries are exhausted, the data team gets a Slack notification that same morning, before leadership opens a dashboard built on stale or half-built data.

When someone reports a number looks wrong, the troubleshooting sequence follows the pipeline's own dependency order: did the DAG run succeed, did dbt_test pass, and only then, query history for the actual query Power BI ran. Checking in this order finds the real cause far faster than guessing at the DAX measure first.
Real Snowsight query output grouping credit consumption by warehouse -- exactly the kind of query that confirms DRIFTWOOD_ETL_WH and DRIFTWOOD_BI_WH are costing what you'd expect, separately.
And the Admin Warehouses tab shows each warehouse's real size and state at a glance -- the first place to check if a warehouse is running longer, or more often, than it should.
Next lesson: disaster recovery with Time Travel and Fail-safe -- what actually happens when a mistake, not just a cost spike, hits this platform.
